analysis.one_liner: Reopens Arctic waters to offshore oil drilling and funds Alaska tribal climate projects with the revenue.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee from April 2017 until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have erased a 2016 presidential order that withdrew large parts of the Arctic Ocean from oil and gas leasing. It would have required yearly lease sales off Alaska's coast, given oil companies 20-year lease terms in the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas, and sent a growing share of drilling royalties to Alaska, its coastal towns, and a new fund to help Alaska Native tribes deal with climate change — including relocating villages that are washing into the sea. It never received a committee vote and died when the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain guaranteed access to new leases in the Beaufort, Chukchi, and Cook Inlet planning areas, with 20-year initial terms and extensions for existing leases in the harsh Arctic offshore. The State of Alaska and its coastal communities would get a share of royalties (7.5% for 2017–2027, rising to 30% from 2028) plus workforce training money. Alaska Native tribes would get a Tribal Resilience Fund of up to $200 million a year for climate adaptation, with at least 90% going to construction projects such as relocating eroding villages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies, Alaska, and Native tribes

how_it_helps.text: The bill nullifies the December 20, 2016 presidential memorandum that withdrew Arctic outer Continental Shelf areas from mineral leasing, and bars any similar future presidential withdrawal of those areas.

It requires the Interior Department to hold one lease sale per year in each of a new Nearshore Beaufort Sea Planning Area and the Cook Inlet Planning Area in fiscal years 2018–2020, and to include at least three sales in each of the Beaufort and Chukchi planning areas in every five-year leasing program.

It gives oil and gas leases beyond 3 nautical miles of Alaska's coast in the Beaufort and Chukchi areas a 20-year initial term, and lets current leaseholders extend existing leases to 20 years — a longer runway to explore and develop in expensive, hard-to-reach waters.

It rewrites the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act revenue formula so that Alaska, its coastal political subdivisions, the North Slope Science Initiative, workforce training programs, and a new Tribal Resilience Fund receive shares of offshore energy revenues (with Alaska's share rising from 7.5% to 30% after fiscal 2027).

It creates a Tribal Resilience Program with grants of up to $200 million per year to Indian tribes for climate adaptation — including relocating villages threatened by coastal or river erosion, repairing permafrost damage, and building evacuation infrastructure — with at least 90% of program money required to go to capital projects.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury would keep a smaller share of royalties (75% initially, falling to 50% from 2028). The broader public would bear the environmental cost of drilling in the Arctic Ocean: greenhouse gas emissions from new oil production, and the risk of a spill in remote, ice-covered waters where cleanup is difficult and fishing and subsistence communities depend on the coast.
analysis.who_pays_short: Treasury and the public, via climate and spill risk

drawbacks.text: The bill ties tribal climate-adaptation money to offshore drilling: the Tribal Resilience Fund is filled from drilling revenues (2.5% of qualified revenues through 2027, 12.5% thereafter), and its appropriations backstop is capped at $200 million a year — so tribes get the funding only if the drilling the bill mandates actually produces revenue or Congress appropriates the difference.

It permanently constrains future presidents: the bill nullifies the 2016 withdrawal and any similar future presidential action, and requires lease sales in every five-year program regardless of changing conditions — locking the Beaufort, Chukchi, Nearshore Beaufort, and Cook Inlet areas into the leasing schedule.

The public takes on the environmental risk of Arctic offshore drilling — oil production in ice-covered remote waters, with the bill directing even the science program covering the Beaufort and Chukchi seas to fund workforce training for oil and gas pipelines and infrastructure.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a genuine trade-off bill, not a giveaway dressed up as help: the tribal resilience program is a real, large benefit to Alaska Native communities facing erosion and permafrost loss, but it is funded by — and politically tied to — opening the Arctic Ocean to oil drilling. Anyone who supports drilling gets tribal climate money as part of the package; anyone who opposes Arctic drilling loses the tribal funding too. There is no path in the bill to fund tribal resilience without the drilling.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee in April 2017 and was never voted on there or on the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Lisa Murkowski introduced the bill on April 6, 2017 'for herself and Mr. Sullivan' — two Alaska Republicans — and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action was taken: the committee never held a markup or vote, and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

Because the bill never became law, the December 2016 presidential memorandum withdrawing Arctic outer Continental Shelf areas from mineral leasing was not nullified by statute, and no new mandatory Arctic lease sales were created.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, Arctic waters were not statutorily reopened to mandatory leasing — no new leases were created, and no drilling revenue stream was established. Oil companies lost a shot at new Beaufort and Chukchi leases; Alaska tribes gained no new resilience fund; the Treasury kept its full royalty share.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No new Arctic leases; waters stayed withdrawn

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only two known supporters, both Alaska Republicans, and never reached a vote, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition is visible in the record.

industries.note: The bill guarantees annual lease sales off Alaska and gives companies 20-year lease terms and extensions in the Beaufort and Chukchi Seas, a long investment horizon in high-risk Arctic waters. The public would share some of the revenue but bear the climate and spill-risk costs of new production.

The bill creates a Tribal Resilience Fund of up to $200 million a year for climate adaptation, with at least 90% for capital projects such as relocating eroding villages. The funding stream, however, is drawn from offshore drilling revenues.

industries.industry: Alaska state and coastal local governments
industries.note: The bill routes a share of offshore royalties to the state (rising to 30% after 2027) and to coastal political subdivisions, plus money for workforce training and pipeline rights-of-way.
